original_question: On which chromosome is the mutated gene located that causes a hereditary form of lymphedema presented as a unilateral lower extremity lymphedema, which may also be accompanied by hydrocele, and which was described by the namesake physician in late 19th century?

final_qi.question: On which chromosome is the mutated gene located that causes a hereditary form of lymphedema presented as a unilateral lower extremity lymphedema, which may also be accompanied by hydrocele, and which was described by the namesake physician in late 19th century?
final_qi.long_answer: The hereditary lymphedema described by William Milroy (Milroy disease) is caused by mutations in the FLT4 gene that encodes the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-3 (VEGFR-3). The FLT4 gene is located at cytogenetic band 5q35.3 on chromosome 5; thus, the pathogenic mutation underlying this form of congenital unilateral lower-extremity lymphedema (often with associated hydrocele) resides on chromosome 5.

final_answer.long_answer: Milroy’s hereditary lymphedema—first reported by William F. Milroy in 1892—can present as unilateral swelling of a lower limb and is frequently accompanied by a hydrocele in affected males. The condition is caused by heterozygous mutations in the FLT4 (VEGFR-3) gene, which is located on the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q35). Thus, the pathogenic mutation responsible for this form of hereditary lymphedema lies on chromosome 5.
